items.title: 22.6.2 Reactions of the Aromatic Ring in Phenols

source_refs.note: Topic 22.6.2 with Quick Check 22.5, answered (PDF 96-97); the equations are redrawn. The book's '2 phenol' nitration equation is given per molecule. The exercises (PDF 98-100) are not part of the lesson body. Answers need review.

blocks.text: The oxygen of phenol's -OH group donates electron density into the ring: one of its lone pairs overlaps with the ring's pi system and becomes delocalised. The extra electron density makes the ring more open to electrophilic attack (activated), and the -OH group directs incoming electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

Phenol is nitrated by dilute nitric acid at room temperature, giving a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol: C6H5OH + HNO3 -> HOC6H4NO2 + H2O. With concentrated nitric acid the product is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: C6H5OH + 3HNO3 -> C6H2(NO2)3OH + 3H2O. Benzene, by contrast, needs a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids warmed to between 25 and 60 C; phenol, being more reactive, needs milder conditions.

blocks.alt: Two reactions, both starting from phenol at room temperature. 2 phenol with dilute HNO3(aq) gives 2-nitrophenol + 4-nitrophenol, braced as 'mixture of products formed', + 2H2O. Phenol with conc. HNO3(aq) gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol + 3H2O.
blocks.caption: Nitration of phenol with dilute and concentrated nitric acid (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 96).

blocks.text: Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature: it decolourises the orange bromine solution and forms a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr. Benzene is brominated only by pure bromine (not a solution) with an anhydrous AlBr3 catalyst; phenol reacts readily with bromine water and no catalyst.

blocks.alt: Phenol + 3Br2 (orange solution), room temperature over the arrow, gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate), with Br at positions 2, 4 and 6, + 3HBr.
blocks.caption: Bromination of phenol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 97).

blocks.text: 1-naphthol has a hydroxyl group at position 1 of naphthalene. As in phenol, the -OH group donates electrons and activates the naphthalene ring to electrophilic substitution, directing electrophiles to positions 2 and/or 4; positions 9 and 10 cannot be substituted because they carry no hydrogen. With bromine in ethanoic acid, 1-naphthol gives 2-bromo-1-naphthol and 4-bromo-1-naphthol.

blocks.alt: 1-naphthol: two fused benzene rings with OH at position 1. The ring positions are numbered 1 to 8 round the outside, with 9 and 10 at the two shared carbons.
blocks.caption: 1-naphthol is a phenolic compound (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 97).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed label '1-naphtol' is misspelt; it is 1-naphthol.

blocks.alt: Numbered 1-naphthol, with Br2 over the arrow and CH3COOH under it, gives 2-bromo-1-naphthol + 4-bromo-1-naphthol.
blocks.caption: Bromination of 1-naphthol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 97).

items: The reaction of phenol with bromine water is used to identify phenol. What is seen, and what is the systematic name of the product?
Which is nitrated more easily, benzene or phenol, and why?
Write the equation for the nitration of 1-naphthol.
